title: Sound is the part of AI-built games that still feels unfinished. How are you handling audio?
author: shanebrumback
selftext:
Agents can get the visuals and gameplay of a browser game surprisingly far in a few sessions. Audio is often the piece that lags behind: missing footsteps, one gunshot sample on repeat, music that cuts off on level change, or sounds that won't play until the player clicks because of browser autoplay rules.

Some approaches I've seen people use:

\- Generating sound effects and music with AI audio tools, then having the agent wire them up.

\- Using free sound libraries and letting the agent handle only the playback code.

\- Having the agent synthesize simple effects in code with the Web Audio API instead of loading files.

\- Building a small audio manager first (pooling, volume groups, random pitch variation) before adding any sounds.

\- Leaving audio until the very end, after gameplay is locked.

For people building games with AI:

1. Where do your sounds come from right now?

2. Do you let the agent decide when and where sounds play, or do you place them yourself?

3. Has anyone gotten positional 3D audio working well in a browser game?

4. How much does sound change how players react to your game?

comments.author: imlo2
comments.body:
I've tried to to use a few approaches:  
  
1. Used Scenario via MCP. It does cost but they have bunch of audio models there. But that costs money.  
  
2. Also, I've now used ComfyUI via API locally, and I've built my own wrapper for YuE2 for music (there's also official now), and then use variety of existing audio models like Stable Audio. It's surprisingly good at times for sound effects, comparable to what Suno can create (depending on content.) This is much more easier than it sounds; doesn't take long to set up especially if you have any clue how Comfy works, just ask the agent to set it up for you.   
  
3. You can also have the models (Code/Claude) build synthetic sounds like you suggested, I've used that too.

4. Build tooling you can copy over to new projects, like audio analysis toolkit, and there's already good tools/libraries for Python, you can build on top of those. I had agent create tools which helped fix clipped tails of sound effects, remove other artifacts etc. 

5. You can use videos and other more exotic ways to generate effects; I've used Kling and other cheaper models for this - generate with audio in low resolution, and then hand over the material to agent, which will then use demucs and other audio processing tools to extract the effects. Screams, punches, explosions, etc. cinema-style sfx come out much better than from specialized audio generators.

6. You can also experiment with the video to audio with MMAudio via ComfyUI; there the route would be generate video of something happening, and then have MMAudio generate audio for it, and extract the audio. But it's not that great quality model, results are often quite mediocre.

7. There are paid well-established tools like Game Synth, which you could look into, and just do a keyword "procedural SFX" or such to find information on this topic.

comments.body:
The old fashioned way. Music is one thing that AI can do well, but music is one thing I won't do with AI. I want my music to have soul in my games, and AI can't recreate that feeling quite yet.

Sound effects though, elevenlabs is probably the best one. I haven't seen any that come quite as close. You can also do a lot of sound effects on local LLMs from hugging face, etc.

replies.author: animatedeez
replies.body: It can easily have soul etc etc. I wrote and played my songs in my closet with blankets on the walls. Then I used ai to cover/master it. It uses the exact same notes and playing style. But it sounds super crystal clear/sharp and professional. Idk but I think because its real notes and songs I myself made ai has a far easier time making it sound professional. Anything I just tried to generate for funzies or tests sounded awful.

replies.author: Abject-Constant784
replies.body:
So in this case it's just running your personally played music through filtering and audio adjustments rather than fully "recreating" it. And that's why it keeps its "soul".

Generating music from nothing though almost always has no soul. Without using prior audio to build its music off of, AI music is lifeless. And if you use another person's audio in making your own and it's too close to theirs, you're in for a potential lawsuit.

comments.author: Scrapmiles
comments.body: I'd go with the small audio manager first, since it gives the AI a single place to route every sound through instead of scattering play() calls around the codebase. For the autoplay issue, a practical tip is to create or resume the audio context on the first player input (like the start button) and queue any sounds requested before that. Do you find AI-generated SFX hold up in a mix, or do you end up normalizing and layering them by hand?

comments.author: Weaves87
comments.body:
1. Searching through [freesound.org](http://freesound.org) or buying sfx packs from itch.io. There are some diamonds out there. I haven't had much success with sfx generated by AI, just don't think it's there yet when there's so much quality floating around out there on asset stores

2. I tell the agent exactly where I want the sound to play, agents aren't very good at evaluating game feel, and sounds are *critical* to game feel. The agent can add the code to play the sound, but all the mixing and balancing I do 100% myself

3. Haven't tried 3D in the browser yet

4. Sound is absolutely critical. Nothing takes a player out of a game more than shitty sound. Players will forgive shitty graphics if you have exceptional sound, but great graphics with shitty sound takes them right out of the experience

Sound is imo one of those things that is absolutely non-negotiable if you want your game to feel good to play. I just cannot think of a game that has shitty sound that I enjoy playing

comments.author: metalblessing
comments.body:
On my first game for simple sound effects I would find royalty free sounds on the web, and also used ElevenLabs to generate some of the more specific sounds. 

On my 2nd game (which is currently shelved until I feel like working on it again) I successfully experimented with "Reactive Music" I generated an overworld track for my space rpg when exploring, and I extracted the stems and saved two versions. One original and one with the drum track removed. 

I played the drumless track for a relaxing exploration, but as soon as a battle began it would switch to the original with drums. 

The way I accomplished this was by first having it build an audio manager, and have it play both tracks simultaneously at all times with one muted. When a battle began it gradually crossfades into the 2nd already running track for a seamless transition, and fades back afterwards. I also had it add a timing gate where if the track ends they both are stopped and started simultaneous to avoid any sync issues.

It was pretty slick. Very similar to the reactive music in Doom 2016 and Doom Eternal

comments.author: Bitwizarding
comments.body:
I know that samples are usually the answer for quality (bought, recorded or ElevenLabs). However, I love trying to use code to try to achieve sounds. I made a browser sound lab that uses nodes with oscillators, gain, filters, envelopes and so on which can be really useful for sounds that need adjustment like an engine going from idle to full throttle and back.

I find it a fun challenge to synthesize sounds. Sometimes I have AI generate sounds and some are fine and other times they are horrible. For example, it made a sound for a small creek and it was hissing. It might have been okay for a ocean with a lot of waves. I had it build me a lab with about 20 sliders and I was able to find the right sound.
